paragraphs: Harbeh azharot hizhira tora bishratzim. vehaokel sheretz hammayim, chayyab arba malquyot; vesheretz haaretz - chamesh malquyot; vesheretz haop, kizbubin vekayyotze - shesh malquyot. umetammeim et hannepesh, diktib (vayyiqra y, mg): "venitmetem bam".

clarification.explanation: The Torah warns many times against eating creeping creatures, and establishes different lash penalties depending on the type of creature: one who eats a water-creeping creature (such as forbidden worms or fish) is liable for four sets of lashes; one who eats a land-creeping creature (crawling on the ground) — five sets of lashes; and one who eats a fowl-creeping creature (such as flies) — six sets of lashes. Beyond the penalty of lashes, eating creeping creatures also defiles a person's soul, as the Torah states, "and you shall become impure through them."
takeaways: Eating creeping creatures is severely forbidden, with varying lash penalties depending on the type (water/land/fowl), and it also defiles the soul.

paragraphs: Tolaim haggedelim bayyammim ubannechalim ubammayim hannobein, asurin mishshum sheretz hammayim; abal tolaim haggedelim bammayim shebbakkelim, vaasher beborot shichin umearot sheenam nobein, veken babberekot gedolot sheen lahem motze umuba, hare ellu muttarim kol zeman shello pereshu chutz labbor o chutz lakkeli. veken hu haddin lishar mashqim shebbakkelim, name muttarim kol zeman shello pereshu chutz lakkeli; vaapillu im pereshu laddopen mibbipnim o ledopen hakkeli mibbipnim, muttarim; dekol zeman shello pereshu laachore hakkeli, la miqqere sheretz haaretz; abal im pereshu laachore hakkeli veal sepato mibbachutz, o min habbor velachutz, asurin mishshum sheretz haaretz; yaan ki tekep kesheppereshu mimmeqom giddulam, niqreu sheretz haaretz. velaken kol ir shebbah hattolaim metzuyim bammayim shebbeborot - hen hannobein, hen hamkunnasim - asur liqnot pat mippalter goy beir zo, ki haggoy lash haissa belo sinnun; sheggam beotam sheen nobeim, yesh lachush sheppereshu kannizkar. veken name en lishtot sham mashqeh haqqaho (qapeh) shel haggoyim mittaam haamur. veayyen "peri chadash" umachaziq beraka.

clarification.explanation: Worms that grow in the sea, in rivers, and in flowing spring water are forbidden under the prohibition of "water-creeping creatures." But worms that grow in standing water found in vessels, in pits, in water cisterns, or in caves with no flow, and likewise in large closed pools — are permitted as long as they have not emerged ("exited") beyond the boundary of the pit or vessel in which they grew. The same law applies to other beverages in vessels — permitted as long as they have not left the vessel, and even if the worm is on the inside wall of the vessel, it is permitted — since only emerging outward (beyond the vessel, onto its outer rim) renders it forbidden as a "land-creeping creature." Therefore, in any city where worms are found in cistern water — whether flowing or standing — it is forbidden to buy bread there from a gentile baker, since he kneads the dough without filtering the water, and even in standing water there is concern a worm may have emerged outward. For the same reason, one should not drink coffee prepared by gentiles there.
takeaways: Worms grown in standing cistern/vessel water are permitted as long as they have not left the vessel or pit.
In a city where worms are found in the water, one should not buy bread or coffee prepared by a gentile without filtering, out of concern the worms have already emerged.

paragraphs: "p sheamarnu: tolaim shebbammayim, shebbakkelim veshebbabbur shehem mekunnasin shello pereshu, muttarim min hattora - mikkol maqom asurim midderabbanan mishshum "bal teshaqqetzu" (vayyiqra y, mg) im boleam lebaddam, dehaynu sheyyaknis rosho labbor o lakkeli, veyibla hattola bepiv min hammayim; abal im bolean im hammayim beyachad, en bazeh mishshum "bal teshaqqetzu", deeno nimas beenayv, kevan sheen bolea hattola bipne atzmo, ella yored letok piv im hammashqin. umihu, im beemet meise leh apillu shebboleam im hammashqeh, yesh bazeh issur "bal teshaqqetzu". velaken chabit shel mayim sheyyesh bahem tolaim hammetzuyim bammayim sheqqorin bearbe "alaq" (aluqa, tolaat hammayim): im zeh ha"alaq" hu min hannahar, asur mishshum sheretz hammayim; abal im nithavva venaasa betok hechabit atzmah, muttar min haddin lishtot mayim "p sheyyesh betok hammayim "alaq", kevan denithavva bammayim betok hechabit vaadayin lo peresh. umishshum "bal teshaqqetzu" name lekka, kevan dela shate lehu lebaddam, ella shoteh im hammayim. vaapillu shennotel hammayim min hechabit bikli, la chashib pereshu, ella chashib hakkeli meqom ribbitayhu, mippene shehem gadelu bakkeli shehu hechabit; vekevan dezeh keli vezeh keli, chashib keillu odam bikli rishon; msh"k haggedelim babbor, asur littol hammayim min habbor bikli velishtot, dela chashib meqom rebitayhu bikli zeh sheshshoteh bo, mippene shehem gadelu betok habbor, veatta hem munnachim bikli. mihu poh irenu bagdad, shemmebiin hammayim minnehar chiddeqel – en matzuy tolaim bammayim shebbenahar kelal veiqqar; veraq achar shemmannichin hammayim bechabit babbayit, yithavvu bahem tolaim ellu sheqqorin bearbi "alaq". veim kol zeh nohagin poh irenu lesannen hammayim shebbechabit im yimmatze bahem "alaq" mikkamma teamim: haechad, demeisi lehu, ap-al-pi shehem baim bappeh im hammayim, vekivvun demeisi lehu, ikka issur "bal teshaqqetzu". vehashsheni – chosheshin shemma yannichu meellu hammayim betok keli sheeno amoq, deaz epshar sheyyiprosh zeh ha"alaq" al sepat hakkeli veyachazor letok hammayim; ubazeh neesar min haddin, mishshum deperesh al sepat hakkeli mibbachutz. vehashshelishi – shemma yishshaer tola echad mizzeh ha"illeq" dabuq bakkeli shehinnichu bo hammayim gam achar shennishpak hammayim mimmennu; veim yittenu beoto hakkeli tabshil, yitareb hattola hahu im hattabshil, veate limkalla beenah lebaddo. umeachar shetteamim ellu shel hamminhag chazaqim hem – lekak kol adam tzarik lehizzaher kesheyyimtza "alaq" betok chabit shel mayim kaamur leel, shetztzarik lesanneno, velo yishteh beli sinnun.

clarification.explanation: Although it was established that worms in vessel/cistern water that have not left their place of growth are Torah-permitted, there is nevertheless a rabbinic prohibition — under "you shall not make yourselves detestable" (forbidding one to disgust and debase oneself by eating something repulsive) — if one swallows the worm by itself, that is, when he puts his head into the pit or vessel and swallows the worm directly from the water. But if he swallows it together with the water (that is, without noticing, as part of drinking the water), there is no prohibition of "you shall not make yourselves detestable," since it is not explicitly repulsive to him. Nevertheless, if the matter is truly repulsive to him even when swallowed together with the water, there is a prohibition in this. In the case of a barrel of water with "alaq" (leech) type worms: if the worm came from a river — it is forbidden as a water-creeping creature; but if it formed inside the barrel itself — the water may be drunk by strict law, even containing the "alaq," since it has not left its place of growth. Even if the water is drawn from the barrel into another vessel, this is still considered the same place of growth and not an "exit." By contrast, worms that grew in a cistern — it is forbidden to draw the water into a vessel and drink it, since then it is no longer considered their place of growth. In Rabbi Yosef Chaim's locale (Baghdad) it was customary to filter the water from the barrel if "alaq" was found in it, for three reasons: (a) the matter is repulsive even when swallowed with the water; (b) concern the worm might float to the rim of a shallow vessel and return to the water, which would then be considered as having "exited"; (c) concern a worm might remain stuck in the vessel after the water is poured out, and later mix into food.
takeaways: Worms in vessel/cistern water that have not exited are Torah-permitted, but swallowing them alone (not with the water) is rabbinically forbidden under "you shall not make yourselves detestable."
It was customary to filter water containing "alaq" (leech) worms for several reasons of stringency, even when technically permitted.

paragraphs: Bekol hachatzerot shel poh irenu bagdad y", matzuy beer mayim chayyim shehem mayim nobein, uberubbam matzuy tolaim ellu sheqqorin "alaq"; veellu asurim mishshum sheretz hammayim, v"p shello pereshu, kevan dehem nobein. vekol baale-battim darkan lehaddicha habbasar vekol kele akila beellu hammayim, al-ken tzerikin lizzaher lesannen otam techilla, sheim lo yesanneno hammayim, az nidbaq hattola babbasar ubekelim, veatu lemekeleh beeneh; veyadua hu dibriyya lo batela apillu beelep; veim ken, tolaim ellu en betelim battabshil.

clarification.explanation: In every courtyard in the city of Baghdad there is a well of living (flowing) water, and "alaq" worms are usually found in them. These worms are forbidden as "water-creeping creatures" even without leaving the water, since this is flowing (not standing) water, where the law is more lenient. Since homeowners are accustomed to rinsing meat and eating utensils in this water, one must be careful to filter it before use — since if not filtered, the worm might stick to the meat or utensils and be eaten by mistake as an actual whole creature, and it is a known rule that a worm (a "creature") is not nullified even among a thousand (that is, it is not nullified in the majority, unlike most forbidden substances).
takeaways: Flowing water (such as wells in Baghdad homes) commonly contains "alaq" worms forbidden under water-creeping creatures — one must filter before rinsing meat and utensils.
A worm (a "creature") is not nullified even in a large majority, so even a small concern requires care.

paragraphs: Kol chometz yesh bo tolaim daqqim meod, sheen nirim ella im ken tittenehu betzintzenet neqiyya, vetannichehu al hachallon bemaqom shehashshemesh zorachat, veaz nirin hattolaim; lekak en lo taqqana "y sinnun bilbad, ella yebashshelu bishshul shehayyad soledet bo, veachar sheyyarticha yesanneno. ubimot hachorep, yebashshel visannen beereb-shabbat letzorek hashshabua kullo; veim yishshaer yoter mishshabua, yachazor veyatlia; lekak, bekol ereb-shabbat yesannen; abal baqqayitz shehaavir cham - qarob yoter lehatlia, lekak lo yebashshel visannen, ella raq letzorek chatzi shabua davqa.

clarification.explanation: Vinegar always contains very fine worms invisible to the eye, unless it is poured into a clean jar and placed on a sunny windowsill — where they then become visible. Since filtering alone does not suffice (they are too small to be caught), the vinegar must be boiled to a burning heat and only then filtered. In winter, when the air is colder, one may boil and filter once on the Sabbath eve and use it all week, since if it sits more than a week, worms will re-form in it. In summer, when the heat causes faster worm formation, boiling and filtering must be repeated at least twice a week.
takeaways: Vinegar contains invisible fine worms — it must be boiled to a burning heat and then filtered (cold filtering alone does not suffice).
In summer, boiling and filtering must be renewed twice a week; in winter, once suffices.

paragraphs: Tolaim haggedelim beperot o biraqot bimchubbar, asurin min hattora mishshum sheretz haaretz, "p shello rachashu velo pereshu. veyesh omerim deeno asur ella ad sheyyirchashu. v"p demaran za"l satam beshulchan aruk debaenan sheyyirchashu, mikkol maqom, kevan derabbu haoserim apillu shello rachashu - haki naqetinan lahalaka, leesor gam belo rachashu, deyesh lehachmir beissur tora; veken hamminhag poh irenu bagdad y".

clarification.explanation: Worms that grew inside fruits or vegetables while still attached to the ground (before picking) are Torah-forbidden as "land-creeping creatures," even if they have not yet moved or emerged from the fruit. Some hold the prohibition applies only if the worms have already moved ("stirred") inside the fruit, and although Maran in the Shulchan Aruch leaned toward this view, nevertheless, since most authorities forbid it even when the worms have not yet moved, this is the practical halachic ruling, in order to be stringent regarding a Torah-level prohibition. And so is the Baghdad custom.
takeaways: Fruits/vegetables infested while still attached to the ground are forbidden even if the worms have not yet moved, as the halachic ruling.

paragraphs: Happolin, darkam lehatlia bimchubbar. velaken "p shehammaqom dachuq ubevadday lo rachashu, asurin. vela mibbaya tola beayin, ella apillu im nimtza bahem nequdda shechora, tzarik lechattet velahasirah, shehi asura kattola mammash, yaan demaqom sheyyatchil hattola lehitraqqem, naasa oto maqom shachor. veken nohagim poh irenu lechattet beomeq lehasir nequdda hashshechora.

clarification.explanation: Fava beans tend to become infested while still attached to the ground. Therefore, even though the space is cramped and the worm certainly has not moved within it, they are still forbidden. And not only an actual visible worm — but even a small black dot found on a bean must be picked out and removed, since it is considered an actual worm (the spot where the worm begins to form turns black). This is the Baghdad practice — to dig deep and remove the black dot.
takeaways: Fava beans require careful examination: even a small black dot is considered a sign of a worm and must be picked out and removed.

paragraphs: Hatteenim, veqishshuin sheqqorin bearbe "keyaer" (melapepon matzuy), veken otam sheqqorin "tarozi" (melapepon daq meorek) - darkan lehatlia bimchubbar; veken peri sheqqorin bearbe "kuk" (aparseq), veken pol hammitzri sheqqorin "lubbeya" (sheuit missug "rubbeya"), veken kerub sheqqorin "lehaana" (kerub haqqelach baal alim), veken hachzarat sheqqorin "kes" (chasa) - kol ellu darkan lehatlia bimchubbar, veen leakelam belo bediqa. gam od hakkarpas vehikratti, vegam mah sheqqorin "mdnvs" (ptrvzylyh), matliin bimchubbar, veen leakelam belo bediqa. vehealim shel hatztzenon sheqqorin "pg'l", tzerikin bediqa heteb. veyesh yeraqot shennimtza bahem tolaim daqqim harbeh veqasheh lebadeqan, vehem mah sheqqorin "salleq" (saleqa ale salleq) umah sheqqorin "nina" - shomer napsho yirchaq mehem. upoh irenu okelim zeh ha"salleq", veomerim shebbodeqin oto; vire shamayim yesallequ mibbeto velo yabo al shulchano. ubebetenu lo yikkanes huslaq lemaakol; veraq berosh-hashshana yabiu oto al hashshulchan liroto bilbad, bishbil habbaqqasha shebbahem. vaale gepanim, kebar asarum rabbane aram-tzoba yagen alehem elohim legamre, velo yoil lahem bediqa; veken poh irenu bagdad nohagim bahem issur. veyesh poh irenu yaraq sheqqorin "rshd" (eseb bar charip), vehu gadel bammidbar, ulekak qorin oto bearbe "rshd alber"; veyesh bene-adam omerim ki lo yimmatze bo tolaim, veraq "rshd" shezzorein bagginna yimtza bo tolaim; vezeh sheqer! sheggam haggadel meelayv bammidbar yimtza bo tolaim vetzarik bediqa. veken yaraq sheqqorin bearbe "kebag" (eseb ketablin likbisha), vedarkan likbosh oto gam bazeh yimmatze tolaim vetzarik bediqa. vehakkimon shekichi bo tolaim harbeh betok haggargerim kemo shekkatab ha"peri chadash", al-ken bebetenu en okelim kimmun kelal veiqqar. veyaraq sheqqorin bearbe "btng" (eseb merappe, missug hamnutteh), katabnu dehu matlia bimchubbar; veetzlenu bebetenu mashhin oto y"b chodesh, veaach"k okelim oto.

clarification.explanation: A number of well-known fruits and vegetables become infested while still attached to the ground, and therefore require thorough examination before eating: figs, cucumbers ("khiyar" and "ta'aruzi"), peaches ("khokh"), rubiyah-type beans ("lubiyah"), cabbage ("lahana"), lettuce ("khass"), celery, leeks, and parsley. Radish leaves ("fajl") also require thorough examination. There are vegetables whose worms are so fine and difficult to check — such as beets ("silq") and mint — that a God-fearing person should keep them entirely away from his home. In Baghdad it was customary to eat beets, claiming they check them, but Rabbi Yosef Chaim advises the God-fearing to avoid it, and in his own home he entirely avoids beets as food, bringing it to the table only on Rosh Hashanah to look at (for the signs/requests of Rosh Hashanah). Grape leaves were entirely forbidden by the rabbis of Aleppo, with no benefit from examination at all — and so is the Baghdad custom as well. The vegetable "rashad," growing wild in the desert — some claim it has no worms unlike the cultivated garden variety, but this is a mistake; even the wild-growing kind requires examination. The pickled vegetable "kabaj" contains worms and requires examination. Cumin ("kimon") commonly contains many worms inside the kernels, and therefore in his home cumin is not eaten at all. The vegetable "batanj" (a mint type) becomes infested while attached, and therefore in his home it is left for twelve months before being eaten.
takeaways: A long list of fruits and vegetables commonly harbor worms and require examination: figs, cucumber, peach, beans, cabbage, lettuce, celery, leek, parsley, radish leaves, and more.

Beets and mint are extremely difficult to check, and the God-fearing should avoid them; grape leaves are entirely forbidden even with examination; cumin is entirely avoided in Rabbi Yosef Chaim's home.

paragraphs: Perot shechezqatan shello lehatlia bimchubbar ella raq betalush - im hitliu betalush, muttarim; dela asera tora ella "sheretz hashshoretz al haaretz". bammeh debarim amurim? keshello peresh min happeri, abal im peresh min happeri, apillu lo higgia laaretz, ella shemmet baavir qodem shehiggia laaretz, vaapillu lo perash kullo ella miqtzato, o shello perash ella al gabbe happeri o al haggarin shebbetoko, o shepperesh mipperi lapperi belo avir, kegon shehem debuqim yachad, veyatzea hattolaat mizzeh lazeh derek neqeb belo reiyyat avir - bekol hane gavne, din "peresh" yesh lo, veasur mishshum sheretz haaretz; veyesh letola zeh din birya, daapillu beelep lo batel. vaapillu im hattola met betok happeri, veachar shemmet peresh min happeri, gam ken asur, veyesh lo din sheretz hashshoretz. veayyen keneset haggedola, haggahat habbet yosep, sop ot v', uperi chadash uperi toar uminchat yeuddeh vesipte daat veod acharonim.

clarification.explanation: A fruit whose normal way is not to become infested while still attached to the ground, but only after picking (once detached) — if it became infested after picking, it is permitted, since the Torah forbade only "the creeping creature that creeps on the earth," meaning a worm that has "emerged" from the fruit outward. But the following are also defined as having "emerged" (and therefore forbidden): if the worm died in the air before reaching the ground itself, even if only part of it emerged from the fruit, even if it emerged only onto the surface of the fruit or onto the pit inside it (without touching the ground), and even if it passed from one fruit to another through a hole without passing through the outside air (such as fruits stuck together). In all these cases, this is considered "emerged" and forbidden as a land-creeping creature, and the worm has the status of a "creature" that is not nullified even among a thousand. Even if the worm died inside the fruit and only afterward emerged from it — its law is still that of a forbidden "creeping creature."
takeaways: A fruit that normally becomes infested only after picking is permitted if the worm is still inside; but if it "emerged" from the fruit in any way (even partially, even dead) — it is forbidden, and not nullified at all.

paragraphs: Yesh omerim dela aserinan beperesh, ella im ken yadanu beberur shepperesh, abal im raq nimtza betok happeri velo rainu shepperesh, "p shehu chay vechoro naqub lachutz, muttar. vela chayeshinan shemma peresh vechazar; ken hu daat maran za"l beshulchan aruk. veyesh oserin bechoro naqub lachutz, dilma perash vechazar; veyesh lachush ledaat haoserin; ubiprat shekkatab rama" za"l shekken nahagu. upoh irenu bagdad y" hamminhag pashut leesor bechoro naqub lachutz.

clarification.explanation: Some hold that the prohibition due to "emerging" applies only when it is clearly known the worm has emerged from the fruit; but if the worm is found only inside the fruit and we have not seen it emerge — it is permitted, even if it is alive and its exit hole is open toward the outside, with no concern that it may have emerged and returned inside. This is Maran's view in the Shulchan Aruch. Some forbid it even when the hole is open toward the outside, out of concern the worm indeed emerged and returned, and one should be concerned for this view, especially since the Rema wrote this is the custom. In Baghdad the simple practice is to be stringent and forbid it when the hole is open toward the outside.
takeaways: If the worm is still inside the fruit and we have not seen it emerge — Maran permits it even with the hole open toward the outside; but the accepted custom (including Baghdad) is to be stringent and forbid it.

paragraphs: La amerinan lechalleq ben peresh lelo peresh, ella raq beperot shemmuchzaqin etzlenu sheen matliin bimchubbar ella raq betalush; abal perot deyesh lehistappeq bahem shehitliu bimchubbar, "g deen haddabar barur, hare ellu asurim apillu im lo perash, mishshum dispeq tora lehachmir.

clarification.explanation: The distinction between "emerged" and "not emerged" (intended to be lenient when it is not known the worm emerged) applies only to fruits presumed not to become infested while attached, but only after picking. But for fruits where there is doubt whether they become infested while still attached (even without certainty), they are forbidden even if the worm has not yet emerged, since a doubt in a Torah-level prohibition is resolved stringently.
takeaways: A fruit with doubt whether it became infested while attached (not merely after picking) is forbidden even without knowledge that the worm emerged, under the rule that a Torah-level doubt is resolved stringently.

paragraphs: Tolaim qetannim hannimtzaim baqqemach, asurim; daapillu pereshu ledopen hakkeli mibbipnim, asurim. dedavqa bemayim ushear mashqin sharenan pereshu bipnim, mishshum dehaynu rebitayhu, abal bemaakol la amerinan haynu rebitayhu, vaasurin bekol gavna. velo od, ella apillu im lo sheratzu ella raq beqemach gupah, yesh lahem din "peresh", vaasurin kemo din peresh mipperi lapperi. velaken im hem qetannim, shei epshar lebareram "y harqadat haqqemach, apillu "y napa – neesar haqqemach; abal gedolim, sheepshar lebareram al-yede harqadat haqqemach bannapa - hare zeh meraqqed haqqemach min hattolaim umuttar.

clarification.explanation: Small worms found in flour are always forbidden, even if they have only emerged to the inside wall of the vessel. This differs from water and other beverages, where a worm emerging to the inside wall of the vessel was permitted (since this is considered its natural place of growth), since for food (like flour) one does not say the vessel wall is "their place of growth," and therefore they are forbidden in every case. Furthermore, even if the worms never left the flour itself but only crept within it — they are still considered "emerged" and forbidden, like a worm that passed from fruit to fruit. Therefore, if the worms are so small that they cannot be sifted out of the flour (even through a sieve), the entire flour becomes forbidden. But if the worms are large enough to be separated by sifting, the flour may be sifted and permitted.
takeaways: Worms in flour are forbidden in every case (unlike water, where there is leniency for the natural place of growth).
If the worms can be removed by sifting, the flour is permitted; if too small to sift out, all the flour is forbidden.

paragraphs: Qemach zeh shehitlia, vei epshar lebarero deneesar, asur lemakero legoy, dechayeshinan shemma yimkerennu haggoy leyisrael. vaapillu im nirin hattolaim baqqemach bechush hareut - chayeshinan shemma yeappenu haggoy veyimkerennu leyisrael. vehu haddin bekol mine maakol shehitlia deasur leyisrael, asur lemakero legoy. veayyen keneset haggedola, haggahat habbet yosep, ot p"t. ubehepsed merubbeh yesh lismok al hammattirin limkor legoy meat meat, beinyan shebbevadday lo yimkerennu haggoy leyisrael.

clarification.explanation: Flour that became infested and cannot be sifted (and is therefore forbidden to a Jew) is also forbidden to sell to a gentile, out of concern the gentile might resell it back to a Jew. This concern exists even if the worms are plainly visible in the flour, since there is concern the gentile might bake bread from it and sell it to a Jew in a form that cannot be detected. The same law applies to any kind of food that became infested — if forbidden to a Jew, it is forbidden to sell to a gentile. In a case of great monetary loss, one may rely on the lenient view to sell to a gentile only in small quantities, in a manner where the gentile certainly will not resell it to a Jew.
takeaways: Infested food forbidden to a Jew is in principle forbidden to sell to a gentile, out of concern it will return to a Jew.
In great monetary loss, one may be lenient and sell to a gentile only in small quantities, ensuring it certainly will not return to a Jew.

paragraphs: Qemach zeh shehitlia, muttar lehaakilo leabdo uleshipchato, apillu shemmezonotehem alayv; raq yizzaher shello yeshahennu zeman merubbeh, shello yabo lide taqqala. veyesh chosheshin apillu lizman muat; mihu, im yeappenu veyishneh tzurat happat, shari, devadday lo yikkashel bo kevan dehu meshunneh tzurato umiddekar. veayyen peri chadash umishbetzot zahab.

clarification.explanation: Flour that became infested (and forbidden for a Jew to eat) may be fed to a male or female servant, even if their food is at the homeowner's expense — except one must be careful not to leave this for a long time, so as not to cause a mishap (lest a Jew eat it by mistake). Some are stringent to be concerned about this even for a short time. But if bread was baked from the flour and its form changed, it is certainly permitted, since the form of bread differs from raw flour, and no one would come to stumble.
takeaways: Infested flour may be fed to a servant, but one must be careful not to leave it for a long time.
If bread was baked from it, changing its form, it is entirely permitted, since there is no concern of mistake.

paragraphs: Muttar lehotzi shekar miqqemach shehitlia, veken min temarim o tzimmuqin shehitliu, ki zea bealema hu. veayyen machaziq beraka, ot t"z, vechiqre lb, yoreh dea, siman n"d, veayyen bitshubot haramba"m za"l hanniqraim "peer-haddor", siman qy"d.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to produce beer (a beverage) from infested flour, and likewise from infested dates or raisins, since the resulting beverage is considered only "sweat" (an extracted essence), not as though the worm itself is included in it.
takeaways: It is permitted to make beer from infested dates/raisins/flour, since this is merely an extraction, not the worm itself.

paragraphs: Chittim metullaim - im rubbam metullaim shei epshar lebareram, yimkerem legoy; veim en rubbam metoalim, yebarerem techilla, veaach"k muttar litchanan. veyizzaher lekattechilla litchanan berechayim sheyyesh sham aparkeset, mippene sheim timtze lomar: nishar bahem tolaim achar bediqa, yibrechu bishat techina minnidnud harechayim, veyetzeu derek dupne haaparkeset. ubediabad im en lo rechayim sheyyesh bo aparkeset, muttar litchanan; mishshum daapillu im nishar tolaim - mitrasseqin bitchina, vetu en lahem din birya ubateli; hu kavvanato litchon, velo ba lebattel haissur beyadayim. umehay tama sharenan limkor legoy, vela chayeshinan shemma yeapeh veyimkor leyisrael, mishshum deachar techina nitrasseq hattola ubatel. vechittim ellu dela hitliu rubban, sheamarnu shetztzarik lebareram techilla, haynu lekattechilla abal bediabad im lo beraram vetachnam, muttar. uben haki uben haki, tzarik leraqqed haqqemach achar hattechina. veha desharenan al-yede techina - davqa bechittim dedarkan lehittachen, abal qemach shehitlia, asur letachanu kede sheyyitrassequ hattolaim, deyan mebattelim issur lekattechilla.

clarification.explanation: Infested wheat: if most of the quantity is infested and cannot be sorted out — it should be sold to a gentile (subject to the limitations explained above); if only a minority of the quantity is infested, it should first be sorted and then may be milled. It is preferable to mill with a mill having a "funnel" (strainer), since if worms remain even after checking, they might escape during milling (from the mill's shaking) and exit through the strainer's walls. After the fact, if no such mill is available, it is nevertheless permitted to mill — since even if worms remain, they are crushed during milling and lose the status of a "creature" (which is not nullified), becoming nullified. For this reason it is also permitted to sell this wheat to a gentile without concern he will bake and sell it to a Jew, since after milling the worm is already crushed and nullified. In a case where the wheat was not mostly infested (requiring sorting first) — this is only as the primary practice, but after the fact, if milled without sorting, it is permitted. In every case the flour should be sifted after milling. Important: the leniency of milling applies specifically to wheat (which is normally milled), but flour that has already become infested — it is forbidden to mill it specifically in order to crush the worms and nullify them, since this is a deliberate nullification of a prohibition from the outset, which is forbidden.
takeaways: Wheat with a minority infested: sort then mill (preferably with a strainer mill); with a majority infested — permitted to sell to a gentile without quantity limit, since subsequent milling crushes and nullifies the worm.

Milling crushes and nullifies worms in wheat (even without prior checking, after the fact), but it is forbidden to mill already-infested flour specifically to nullify the worms — this is a deliberate nullification of a prohibition.

paragraphs: En lehattir chittim hannizkarim "y techina veharqada, ella davqa im nimtza bahem tolaim adummim o shechorim, deellu darkan libroach minnidnud harechayim, abal im hitliu betolaim daqqim ulebanim, en lehattir lekattechilla "y techina veharqada hannizkarim. mihu bediabad im tachnam, muttar, devadday nitrassequ venimmochu ubateli; veayyen "peri-toar" seip qatan k"v.

clarification.explanation: The leniency of milling and sifting infested wheat applies specifically to red or black worms, since these tend to escape from the mill's shaking (and therefore have a chance of exiting through the strainer and being disqualified). But if the wheat became infested with fine, white worms, one should not permit milling and sifting as a solution as the primary practice, since they do not escape like the red/black ones. Nevertheless, after the fact, if they were milled anyway, they are permitted, since they certainly were crushed, dissolved, and nullified.
takeaways: The primary leniency for milling is limited to red/black worms (which escape from the mill); for fine white worms, one should not be lenient as the primary practice, though after the fact it is permitted.

paragraphs: Hannapa shel haqqemach, kevan sheyyishshaer bah qemach ben niqbe haariga, veken ben haetz lisarot haariga, veyaggia lahem lachut - yithavveh bah tolaim, ubiprat bime haqqayitz. laken yizzaher lenappetz mimmenna shiyyure haqqemach achar sheoseq bah, veyitleh otah baavir bimqom shelitat hashshemesh; ubekol paam sheyyabo laasoq bah, yibdeqenna heteb. veqodem kamma shanim hebiu leirenu meare hannadeya napa, kullah mibbarzel; vezeh adip tepe, sheyyukal lenappetz mimmenna haqqemach "y hakkaa beyado o baqqarqa; vegam en bah mechabuot sheyyikkanes sham qemach, veyishshaer sham kede sheyyatlia.

clarification.explanation: In a sieve used for sifting flour, flour residue remains between the weave holes and between the wood and the weave's threads, and when moisture reaches it, worms can develop there, especially in summer. One must therefore be careful to shake out the flour residue thoroughly from the sieve after use, and hang it in the air in a sun-exposed place, checking it thoroughly each time before the next use. In the past, a sieve made entirely of metal (iron) was brought to Baghdad, which is preferable since the flour can easily be shaken out of it (by striking it by hand or on the floor), and it has no hiding places where flour could remain and become infested.
takeaways: A sieve must be thoroughly cleaned and shaken out after each use and hung in the sun, to prevent worms forming in residual flour.
A metal sieve is preferable to a wood-and-weave one, since it is easier to clean and has no hiding places.

paragraphs: Debash-temarim sheqqorin bearbe "sillean", sheqqonin min chenvanim debar yom beyomo leakelo uletzorek hattabshil, tzarik lehizzaher lesanneno bachatikat beged techilla, ki yimtza bo nemalim o yattushin, veen nikkarin laenayim. veken hachema, yimtza bah harbeh yattushin deatu mealema; laken haqqoneh yattikenna visannenah. veken debash shennapelu bo nemalim, yechammemu ad sheyyehe nittak, visannenu. umirqachat shennapelu bah nemalim shei epshar lesunnena, en lah taqqana lehashhotah y"b chodesh mishshum deqayma lan: birya sheen bah etzem sheabar aleha y"b chodesh, naaset keapra - dehaka shane, deyesh lehistappeq velomar: ulay haddebash maamid umeqayyem debarim hattemunim betoko; ulehaki gam achar y"b chodesh qayemi beissurayhu.

clarification.explanation: Date honey ("silan") bought daily from shopkeepers for consumption and cooking should first be filtered through cloth, since ants or mosquitoes not visible to the eye may be found in it. Butter also sometimes contains mosquitoes, and therefore one who buys it should melt and filter it. Likewise, honey into which ants have fallen — should be heated until liquid and then filtered. But jam (preserves) into which ants have fallen and which cannot be filtered — has no remedy even by waiting twelve months (despite the rule that "a boneless creature, after twelve months, becomes like dust" and is permitted), since there is concern the sugar preserves and sustains the ants inside it over time, and therefore even after twelve months the jam remains forbidden.
takeaways: Date honey and butter should be filtered/melted-and-filtered before consumption to remove ants/mosquitoes.
Jam with fallen ants that cannot be filtered has no remedy even after waiting 12 months, since the sugar may preserve the ants.

paragraphs: Zebubim hammetilin betzehem bimot hachamma al habbasar, vehem kemo garine chardal lebanim - tzarik libdoq habbasar, ulay yesh bo mizzeh; veim yimmatze, yadicha habbasar yapeh yapeh shello tishshaer apillu achat meellu betze hazzebubin. veayyen machaziq beraka za"l beshem mahara"m ben chabib za"l, yeuyyan sham. upoh irenu bagdad matzuy zeh bime haqqayitz; velipamim yimmatze zeh bebasar hashshoha bachanut etzel mokere habbasar; vetzarik shettitten baalat habbayit datah heteb al zot; vegam babbayit tizzaher lekassot habbasar, velo tannichennu begaluy sheyyachanu alayv hazzebubim.

clarification.explanation: In summer, flies lay eggs on meat, and these eggs look like small white mustard seeds. The meat should be checked for these, and if found, the meat must be thoroughly rinsed so that not a single fly egg remains. In Baghdad this phenomenon is common in summer, sometimes even in meat sitting in butchers' shops; therefore the woman of the house must pay close attention to this, and at home too should take care to cover meat and not leave it exposed, so flies do not land on it.
takeaways: In summer, meat must be checked for fly eggs (resembling small white mustard seeds) and thoroughly rinsed if found.
Meat should be kept covered at home, not left exposed, to prevent flies laying eggs on it.

paragraphs: Nahagu poh irenu bagdad leesor chalab chimmutz sheqqorin bearbe "laban" shehu menuqqab, im hitlia; veken hu haddin haggebina shehitlia, denahagu kisbarat harashba" za"l, ukehaskamat peri chadash v"peri-toar".

clarification.explanation: In Baghdad it was customary to forbid perforated sour milk ("laban") if it became infested, and likewise infested cheese, following the view of the Rashba, with which the "Peri Chadash" and "Peri To'ar" also agreed.
takeaways: Infested sour milk (laban) and cheese are forbidden according to the accepted custom, following the Rashba's view.
